edition.note: The publisher page (Grand Central Publishing, Hachette) gives one hardcover, 304 pages, on sale January 5, 2016, and mentions no revised or later edition. The copyright page of the full text on the Internet Archive reads "Copyright © 2016 by Cal Newport" and "First ebook edition: January 2016". The Lessons follow that text's chapters: Rule #1 to Rule #4. No Lesson rests on later-edition material.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils the start of Rule 1: the four ways to fit deep work into your life. It matters because willpower runs out, so you need a system, not good intentions.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Rule #1 "Work Deeply" opens with the depth philosophies (monastic, bimodal, rhythmic, journalistic). The text says "You have a finite amount of willpower that becomes depleted as you use it." Card unchanged.

rows.claim: Newport's example is Brian Chappell, a busy father and graduate student who wrote his dissertation from 5:30 to 7:30 every morning. The rhythm removed the need to decide.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Text: Brian Chappell, a doctoral candidate, "a father with a full-time job"; he would "wake up and start working by five thirty every morning" and "work until seven thirty". The text adds that he later moved his wake-up earlier. Card unchanged.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils the 4DX part of Rule 1 and the advice to be lazy. It matters because knowing what to do is easy; doing it week after week is the hard part.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Rule #1 holds the sections "Execute Like a Business" (the 4DX disciplines) and "Be Lazy". Card unchanged.

rows.claim: Newport borrows The 4 Disciplines of Execution, or 4DX, a business framework by Chris McChesney, Sean Covey and Jim Huling. It turns depth into a measurable routine.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Text names "The 4 Disciplines of Execution ... (abbreviated, 4DX)"; the notes credit "McChesney, Chris, Sean Covey, and Jim Huling". The four disciplines appear in the order the Lesson uses. Card unchanged.

rows.claim: Apply 4DX to your roadmap: wildly important goal, the first €100 of income from the AI product. Lead measure: deep hours on it, tallied on a card and reviewed every Sunday.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. The €100 goal is the reader's own roadmap, not a figure from the book. The method matches the text: wildly important goal, lead measure of deep hours, a scoreboard of tally marks, and "a weekly review to look over my scoreboard". The Sunday is the Lesson's own choice of day. Card unchanged.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils the end of Rule 1: the shutdown ritual. It matters because a mind that never stops working cannot rest, and tired minds cannot go deep tomorrow.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. The shutdown ritual is described inside "Be Lazy", the last section of Rule #1. Card unchanged.

rows.claim: Newport's shutdown ritual: check email for anything urgent, move every open task onto a list or the calendar, review the calendar and plan tomorrow. Then say a set phrase: "Shutdown complete."
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Text gives the steps in this order: a final look at the e-mail inbox for anything urgent, transfer new tasks to the task lists, skim the lists and the next few days on the calendar, make a rough plan for the next day, then say "Shutdown complete". Card unchanged.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils Rule 2, Embrace Boredom. It matters because focus is a skill you train; a mind that reaches for the phone at every pause cannot go deep on demand.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Chapter heading "Rule #2 Embrace Boredom". Card unchanged.

rows.claim: Clifford Nass at Stanford found that heavy multitaskers were "suckers for irrelevancy." Their brains had trouble filtering out distraction even when they tried to focus.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Text calls Clifford Nass "the late Stanford communications professor" and quotes him: "They're suckers for irrelevancy. They just can't keep on task." The notes give the source as an NPR interview. Card unchanged.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils Rule 3, Quit Social Media, and its craftsman approach to tools. It matters because each app you keep spends the attention you need for ownership.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Chapter heading "Rule #3 Quit Social Media"; it sets out "the craftsman approach to tool selection". Card unchanged.

rows.claim: Newport opens with Baratunde Thurston, a digital media consultant who went offline for 25 days. It did not take him long to adjust to a disconnected life.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Text: "author and digital media consultant Baratunde Thurston ... decided to disconnect from his online life for twenty-five days"; "it didn't take long to adjust to a disconnected life". Card unchanged.

rows.claim: The law of the vital few is the 80/20 rule: a few activities produce most of the results. Low-value tools steal time from the high-value activities.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Text: "The Law of the Vital Few: In many settings, 80 percent of a given effect is due to just 20 percent of the possible causes." Card unchanged.

rows.claim: Quit social media for 30 days without announcing it. Then ask two questions: would the last 30 days have been notably better with this service, and did people care that you were gone?
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Text: "ban yourself from using them for thirty days"; "don't mention online" that you are signing off; the two questions are whether the thirty days would "have been notably better" with the service and "Did people care that I wasn't using this service?" Card unchanged.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils Rule 4, Drain the Shallows, and its time-blocking method. It matters because shallow work expands to fill any day you do not plan.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Chapter heading "Rule #4 Drain the Shallows"; it holds the section "Schedule Every Minute of Your Day". Card unchanged.

rows.claim: Newport opens with Jason Fried's 37signals, the company behind Basecamp, which tried a four-day workweek in summer. Staff got as much done because they cut the shallow work.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Text: in the summer of 2007 37signals (now Basecamp) cut its workweek from five days to four; staff "seemed to accomplish the same amount of work"; it now runs "from May through October". Jason Fried is quoted that fewer hours help "squeeze the fat out of the typical workweek", which Newport reads as shallow work. Card unchanged.

rows.claim: Schedule every minute of your day. On paper, divide the workday into blocks of at least 30 minutes and give every block a task.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Text: "Schedule every minute of your day", on lined paper; "the minimum length of a block should be thirty minutes". Card unchanged.

rows.claim: Ask your boss for a shallow work budget: what share of your time should go to shallow work? Newport says most non-entry-level knowledge workers land at 30 to 50 percent.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Text: "For most people in most non-entry-level knowledge work jobs, the answer to the question will be somewhere in the 30 to 50 percent range". The question is put to the boss. Card unchanged.
